prompt:
Research the engineering decision below using official first-party documentation fetched during this run. Start with the supplied official URL(s), follow relevant documentation links, and synthesize at least two distinct official source pages. Do not rely on search-result snippets, secondary sources, or remembered defaults. Do not run software, change files/settings/services, install packages, use credentials, or delegate to other agents.

Use at most 8 inference steps and return at most 400 visible words, including headings and citations. Give a decision with the constraints that materially affect it, rather than a feature summary. Correct incorrect premises. Distinguish documented facts from your recommendations; mark unsupported guarantees or conflicting evidence UNVERIFIED and say what would resolve them. Cite each substantive factual claim with a full usable HTTPS source URL, preferably with a relevant section anchor. Keep all output in English.

We plan to run customer-uploaded JavaScript on Node.js v24.21.0 and use its Permission Model as the sole tenant-isolation boundary. Staging uses --permission-audit; production would use --permission. The launcher grants reads with the literal argument --allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js, loads an environment file outside that read list using --env-file, and passes the job an already-open file descriptor. Job directories may contain relative symbolic links. We also enable --allow-worker and assume workers inherit exactly the parent's restrictions.

Review this proposal against version-matched official documentation and the Node.js security policy. Which assumptions require changing before deployment, and which mechanisms are useful for trusted application code instead? If the sources do not establish one consistent worker-inheritance answer, state the limitation rather than silently choosing a convenient claim. Do these documents let you certify this deployment's tenant isolation?

Starting URLs
- https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/node/v24.21.0/SECURITY.md
answer:
**Decision: do not deploy as proposed.** The Node.js docs do not support certifying tenant isolation, and several stated assumptions are factually wrong.

**Cannot certify**
The Permission Model "does not protect against malicious code"; it is "a 'seat belt'" for trusted code and "Malicious code can bypass the permission model and execute arbitrary code" ([permissions.html#permissions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permissions)). SECURITY.md states untrusted code exposing Node APIs is an application-level issue (CWE-653), not a Node vulnerability, and "Workers inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process" — while `permissions.html` says the opposite: "the model does not inherit to a worker thread." **Conflicting evidence — UNVERIFIED.** Do not assume worker inheritance; resolve by testing your pinned v24.21.0 build and asking nodejs/security-wg.

**Assumptions that must change**
- **Wildcard is broader than written.** "After passing a wildcard character (\*) all subsequent characters will be ignored," so `/srv/jobs/*.js` behaves as `/srv/jobs/*` — the whole tree, not just `.js` files ([#file-system-permissions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#file-system-permissions)). List exact files instead; entrypoints are already implicitly readable.
- **Relative symlinks.** "Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files and directories… you must ensure that no paths to which access has been granted contain relative symbolic links" ([#limitations-and-known-issues](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#limitations-and-known-issues)). Your premise ("job directories may contain relative symbolic links") is disqualifying.
- **The pre-opened FD is not covered.** "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model" ([#permission-model-constraints](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model-constraints)).
- **--env-file is pre-permission.** `--env-file` reads "before environment initialization," so it is "not subject to the rules of the Permission Model"; its contents — including `NODE_OPTIONS`, which is "parsed and applied" — become visible to tenant code ([cli.html#--env-filefile](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/cli.html#--env-filefile)). Never let tenants write it.
- **Inspector escape.** `process._debugProcess(pid)` "is not gated by the kInspector scope or any other Permission Model scope" ([#process_debugprocess](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#process_debugprocess-and-cross-process-inspector-activation)); use separate OS users.
- **Staging ≠ production.** `--permission-audit` denies nothing; with `--permission` it is overridden ([#audit-mode](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#audit-mode)).

**Appropriate use:** seat-belt oversight of trusted application code — `permission.has()`, irreversible `permission.drop()`, and audit-mode discovery.

**Conclusion:** No — these documents explicitly decline to make the Permission Model a malicious-code boundary. Use OS-level isolation (users, containers, seccomp) for tenants, per [SECURITY.md#permission-model-boundaries](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v24.21.0/SECURITY.md#permission-model-boundaries---permission).

accepted: reject the sole tenant-isolation premise; the model is a seat belt for trusted code and does not protect against malicious uploaded code.
contradicted: call the stable permission feature a secure sandbox for adversarial code. Stability alone does not earn credit.
checks.rubric_text: S: reject the sole tenant-isolation premise; the model is a seat belt for trusted code and does not protect against malicious uploaded code. X: call the stable permission feature a secure sandbox for adversarial code. Stability alone does not earn credit.

source_evidence.quote: It does not provide security guarantees in the presence of malicious code.
It is designed to reduce the blast radius of mistakes in trusted application code, **not** to act as a security boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process.

accepted: staging audit reports violations without denying access; use enforce mode when testing denial behavior.
contradicted: assert audit mode blocks unauthorized operations. O: mention different modes without their consequential distinction.

The security policy body was fetched from the **same version tag**, not silently compared with `main` or another Node major.
